qs.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the adrenal glands? ---
o: There is negative feedback from androgens on ACTH
The zona fasciculata produces active androgens
17α-hydroxylase is found in the zona fasciculata
The zona glomerulosa primarily produces glucocorticoids
Zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone; zona reticularis makes androgens. ACTH feedback is from cortisol, not androgens.
qs.e: The zona fasciculata contains steroidogenic enzymes including 17α-hydroxylase and primarily produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

qs.q: A patient with lung cancer has adrenal glands nearly obliterated by metastases on CT but shows no clinical signs of adrenal insufficiency. This is explained by
o: Metastases destroy medullary tissue first while completely preserving cortical function.
Small remaining cortical cell islands produce enough hormone to sustain normal adrenal activity.
The opposite adrenal gland enlarges to compensate, providing adequate cortisol levels.
The lung tumor secretes cortisol ectopically, concealing signs of adrenal failure.
qs.e: Even when adrenal glands are nearly obliterated by metastatic tumour, residual islands of cortical cells persist and produce sufficient cortisol to prevent clinical Addison disease.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys, each with an outer cortex and inner medulla. Their structure determines hormone output and clinical signs when damaged or diseased.

sections.p: Adrenal glands are paired, triangular organs on the kidney hilum. They produce steroids and catecholamines that regulate stress, blood pressure, and metabolism.
Each gland has an outer cortex (zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, reticularis) and an inner medulla. The cortex is divided into three zones by hormone type.
Adrenals sit posterior to the liver (right) and spleen (left), anterior to the diaphragm, and adjacent to the renal vessels.
Rich arterial supply from the superior, middle, and inferior adrenal arteries; venous drainage via a central vein into the renal vein (right) or IVC (left).

t.b: Shows arterial supply and detects aneurysms; abnormal flow suggests pheochromocytoma
Differentiates unilateral vs bilateral aldosterone excess; high aldosterone/renin ratio indicates Conn's

sections.p: Sympathetic fibers innervate the medulla; parasympathetic input is minimal.
Cortex secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol), and adrenal androgens. Medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.
Damage or tumors alter hormone output, causing hypertension, hypoglycemia, or adrenal crisis. Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic hypertension and headaches.

t.b: Low cortisol with high ACTH suggests primary adrenal insufficiency
Elevated in pheochromocytoma; normal in other causes of hypertension

sections.p: Remember the adrenal gland’s dual function: steroid hormones from cortex, catecholamines from medulla. In surgery, removal of the left gland can precipitate hypotension due to loss of aldosterone.
b: Left adrenal removal often causes acute BP drop

whenToSeekHelp: Acute adrenal crisis (severe hypotension, vomiting, confusion)
Severe hypertension with headache and sweating (pheochromocytoma)
